reason: Any external caller can whitelist arbitrary addresses as swap pairs. This lets an attacker mark their own or a victim's address as a pair, changing which branch of _transferAIS executes. An attacker can use fake pairs to repeatedly trigger the pair-transfer branches, inflate PendingMint, call MarketVault.addMarketValue with arbitrary values, and bypass the pending-burn settlement. If a victim with a pending burn is marked as a pair, the victim's next transfer (including through an approved router) can take the from-pair branch, skipping the normal burn logic and potentially leaving PendingBrun greater than the actual ERC20 balance. Since balanceOf subtracts PendingBrun, this causes balanceOf to revert and can lock the victim's funds. This vulnerability is exploitable by any address without privileges.

vulnerability: PendingBrun overwritten instead of accumulated (burn-tax evasion)
reason: In both pair branches the contract assigns PendingBrun[to] or PendingBrun[from] instead of adding to the existing value. After a large sell sets PendingBrun[from] to 10% of the sale value, the user can make a tiny sell to the pair to overwrite PendingBrun[from] with a near-zero amount. Alternatively, a tiny buy or, with the public setSwapPairs, a tiny transfer from a fake pair can overwrite a large PendingBrun for the recipient. The user can then transfer the actual tokens normally without ever burning the previously accrued amount. This directly defeats the token's burn/tax mechanism and allows users to repeatedly avoid the intended burn.

vulnerability: Pending burn burned from wrong account
reason: In the final branch, the code calls burn(PendingBrun[from]) instead of _burn(from, PendingBrun[from]). The public burn function burns from _msgSender(). Therefore, when _transferAIS is reached through transferFrom and the spender is not the from address, the spender's tokens are burned to clear from's pending burn. This either causes transferFrom to revert if the spender has insufficient AIS, breaking integrations and potentially locking user funds, or it makes the spender pay the burn while from keeps the tokens that should have been burned. An attacker can first create a large PendingBrun for their own address, then call a victim contract that performs transferFrom(attacker, ..., ...) as spender; the victim contract will have its own AIS burned to clear the attacker's pending burn, draining the victim contract if it holds AIS.
